records.name: Green Climate Fund

records.intermediaries: Ministry of Economy and Finance
records.implementers: Public, private, philanthropic

records.scale:
Micro (<USD 10 million) to Large (>USD 250 million)

records.thematic: GCF accepts funding requests on a rolling basis; approvals are generally granted at GCF Board Meetings which occur three times a year.
records.size:
Smallholder farmers and pastoralist communities.
Indigenous peoples and forest-dependent communities in the Amazon and Andes.
Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and community-based enterprises in the bioeconomy.
Rural entrepreneurs and producer cooperatives.
Local and regional governments involved in land-use planning and ecosystem management.
Women and youth participating in sustainable livelihood initiatives.
records.frequency:
Climate-resilient agriculture and livestock management (e.g., climate-adapted grazing, pasture restoration, agroforestry).
Ecosystem restoration and conservation (puna grasslands, peatlands, Amazon wetlands and forests).
Sustainable forest management and avoided deforestation initiatives.
Development of nature-based enterprises and bioeconomy value chains (non-timber forest products, sustainable tourism, agroforestry products).
records.targetGroups:
Entities must secure accreditation by meeting fiduciary standards, environmental/social safeguards, and gender policies. Projects require no-objection letters from NDAs, detailed concept notes, and full proposals emphasizing mitigation/adaptation balance, with at least half of adaptation funds for vulnerable nations.

The GCF’s funding proposal cycle involves several key steps:
Concept Note (optional): Accredited entities (AEs) may submit a concept note to the GCF Secretariat to receive early feedback and ensure alignment with GCF’s mandate and investment criteria
Funding Proposal: The AE, in close coordination with the National Designated Authority (NDA), prepares and submits a full Funding Proposal (FP). This must include a no-objection letter from the NDA and all required technical documentation, including environmental and social assessments
Assessment: After an initial review for completeness, the Secretariat conducts a detailed assessment. The Independent Technical Advisory Panel (iTAP) then evaluates the proposal against six GCF investment criteria and may recommend modifications or conditions
Board Consideration: The Secretariat forwards the FP to the GCF Board for decision. The Board may approve, approve with conditions, or reject the proposal
Legal Arrangements: If approved, the Secretariat and the AE negotiate and sign a Funded Activity Agreement (FAA), which sets the legal framework for project/programme implementation. · Only entities that have been accredited by GCF may apply & access finance directly.
records.activities: Access to GCF resources depends on strong national governance. Countries must have a National Designated Authority (NDA), aligned climate strategies (e.g., NDCs), and accredited entities meeting fiduciary, environmental, social, and gender standards. Accredited Entities (AEs) prepare proposals with NDA endorsement, ensuring balance between mitigation and adaptation, with at least half of adaptation funds directed to vulnerable nations. The funding cycle includes concept submission, Secretariat and Independent Technical Advisory Panel assessment, Board approval, and signature of a Funded Activity Agreement for implementation.

records.name: Global Environment Facility
records.summary: The Global Environment Facility (GEF) is the world’s largest multilateral trust fund providing grants and blended finance to developing countries for projects addressing biodiversity loss, climate change, land degradation, chemicals/waste, and ocean health.
records.intermediaries: UNDP, FAO, UNEP, World Bank, IFAD
records.implementers: Public. GEF-8 is funded by 29 donor governments, including Japan, Canada, Switzerland, Finland, Italy, Norway, New Zealand, and the USA. Since its inception GEF has been funded by a total of 40 donor countries.
records.instruments: National, subnational, jurisdictional, landscape · Climate change mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity conservation, sustainable agriculture, food systems, NbS
records.scale: Current active portfolio numbers from the GEF's operational database, show Peru is associated with 191.3 million USD in national projects and 264.2 million USD in regional/global projects.
records.thematic:
Opportunities for funding typically emerge via implementing agencies in the target countries.
All funding approvals by GEF occur in the twice-yearly Council meetings (usually held in June and December)
records.size:
Smallholder farmers and rural agricultural communities.
Indigenous peoples and local communities managing forests and ecosystems.
Community-based organizations, NGOs, and civil society groups.
Producer associations and local cooperatives involved in sustainable agriculture or forest products.
Local and regional government institutions responsible for land-use planning and ecosystem management.
Women and youth participating in community-based environmental initiatives.
records.frequency:
Ecosystem restoration and conservation (e.g., restoration of dry forests, protection of biodiversity, and ecological corridors in degraded landscapes).
Sustainable land management and climate-resilient agriculture (e.g., agroforestry, silvopastoral systems, sustainable farming practices).
Conservation of agrobiodiversity and traditional agricultural systems in Andean landscapes.
Community-based conservation and sustainable livelihoods through the GEF Small Grants Programme (biodiversity conservation, climate mitigation, and land degradation prevention).
Landscape governance, land-use planning, and strengthening institutional capacity for ecosystem management.
Market access and sustainable value chains for forest and agricultural products.
records.targetGroups:
All projects or programs must fulfill the following criteria to be eligible for GEF funding.

Eligible country: Countries may be eligible for GEF funding in one of two ways: a) if the country has ratified the conventions the GEF serves and conforms with the eligibility criteria decided by the Conference of the Parties of each convention; or b) if the country is eligible to receive World Bank (IBRD and/or IDA) financing or if it is an eligible recipient of UNDP technical assistance through its target for resource assignments from the core (specifically TRAC-1 and/or TRAC-2).
National priority: The project must be driven by the country (rather than by an external partner) and be consistent with national priorities that support sustainable development.
GEF priorities: To achieve the objectives of multilateral environmental agreements, it is required that the GEF support country priorities that are ultimately aimed at tackling the drivers of environmental degradation in an integrated fashion. For this reason, the focal areas (Biodiversity, Climate Change, Land Degradation, International Waters, and Chemicals and Waste) remain the central organizing feature in the GEF-8 Programming Directions and provide countries with the opportunity to participate in selected “Integrated Programs” which aim to address major drivers of environmental degradation and/or deliver multiple benefits that fall under the GEF’s mandate (for more details, see the GEF-8 Programming Directions).
Financing: The project must seek GEF financing only for the agreed incremental costs on measures to achieve global environmental benefits.
Participation: The project must involve the public in project design and implementation, following the Policy on Stakeholder Engagement and the respective guidelines. · Proposals must be submitted through dedicated GEF agencies (e.g. UNEP, FAO, UNDP, UNIDO). Proposals may only be submitted by  government actors, CSOs, NGOs, private sector SMEs, or research institutions.
records.activities: Project eligibility depends strongly on alignment with international environmental conventions and national policy priorities. Proposals must be endorsed by the designated government focal points and demonstrate coherence with existing frameworks—such as National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAPs) or national climate commitments, making a supportive policy environment essential.

records.name: Adaptation Fund

records.intermediaries: UNDP, UNEP, World Bank, IFAD, etc.
records.implementers: Public and private: Primarily financed through voluntary contributions from governments and private donors, plus a 2% share of proceeds from Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) from Kyoto Protocol Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) projects.
records.instruments: National and subnational · Climate change adaptation, biodiversity and ecosystem resilience, climate-resilient agriculture, food systems, NbS
records.scale:
Up to USD 10million per project

Peru has received relatively modest funding from the Adaptation Fund compared to the GEF or GCF, with approved grants totaling around $20 million USD across a handful of projects
records.thematic: Funding requests are accepted on a rolling basis; approvals are granted at Board meetings which occur 2x per year.
records.size:
Smallholder farmers, fishers, and rural livelihoods dependent on climate-sensitive ecosystems.
Indigenous peoples and local communities managing ecosystems and natural resources.
Local and regional governments responsible for climate planning and adaptation investments.
Community organizations and local enterprises involved in climate-resilient livelihoods.
records.frequency:
Ecosystem-based adaptation and nature-based solutions to reduce climate risks (e.g., restoration of ecosystems, watershed protection, and green infrastructure in vulnerable territories).
Climate-resilient livelihoods and diversification of local economic activities to reduce dependence on climate-sensitive sectors.
Climate risk planning and governance (integration of adaptation into local planning, budgeting, and territorial management).
Pilot adaptation interventions such as water management, ecosystem restoration, and hybrid infrastructure for climate resilience.
Capacity building and knowledge management to support climate adaptation policies and scaling of successful solutions.
records.targetGroups: To apply, proposals must be submitted by an accredited implementing entity on behalf of a developing country that is a Party to the Kyoto Protocol, and they must demonstrate clear adaptation benefits, alignment with national adaptation priorities (e.g., NAPs or NDCs), strong environmental and social safeguards, stakeholder participation, and sound financial management. · Funding can only be accessed by accredited National, Regional, or Multilateral Implementing Entities (NIEs, RIEs, MIEs). Proposals mst be endorsed by a country's Designated Authority (usually a government ministry)
records.activities: The  Fund applies a country-driven, direct access model that allows developing countries (Parties to the Kyoto Protocol) to seek financing through accredited implementing entities. This approach strengthens national ownership but also demands robust fiduciary systems, environmental and social safeguards, and institutional capacity. Project proposals must demonstrate clear adaptation benefits, alignment with NAPs or NDCs, and inclusive stakeholder participation. While the Fund promotes institutional empowerment, its effectiveness ultimately depends on countries’ readiness to meet its governance and accountability standards.

records.summary: GIZ is a German development agency that provides services for international cooperation and sustainable development across more than 130 countries.

records.capital: Grants, concessional loans, climate risk insurance

Private sector, civil society, and government agencies (MIDAGRI, MINAM, SERNANP) in energy, water, and forest sectors.
records.frequency:

records.activities: Operates through government cooperation and therefore depends on basic institutional frameworks and bilateral agreements. However, it is unique in that it also actively helps strengthen the enabling environment by building policies, institutions, and governance systems.

records.name: Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA)
records.summary: JICA is a governmental agency that coordinates Official Development Assistance (ODA) for the Japanese government to support socioeconomic development, recovery, and economic stability in developing regions.
records.intermediaries: Implementing partners include microfinance institutions, technical extension and other service providers.
records.implementers: Public. JICA ia primarily funded by the government of Japan.
records.instruments: Landscape, jurisdictional · Climate change mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity, agriculture, food systems, NbS
records.scale: Individual grants provided through the Smallholder Horticulture Empowerment & Promotion (SHEP) approach are typically small (USD 1-5,000)
records.thematic: Regular funding calls, but they are primarily structured around ODA from partner governments, research initiatives, and specific partnership programs rather than open grants for individuals or NGOs.

Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), particularly women-led businesses, via financing through Mibanco.
Rural children and families in vulnerable areas facing malnutrition, plus smallholder farmers in food security programs.
Marginal urban and indigenous communities in Lima and Amazon regions needing sanitation and natural resource access
records.frequency:
Financial access for MSMEs to promote inclusive growth and economic resilience in rural/peri-urban areas.
Nutrition and food security enhancement: reducing child malnutrition through sustainable practices and healthy food systems.
Water/sanitation and disaster management: sanitary improvements in Lima marginal areas, wetland/forest monitoring, seismic housing

records.name: UN Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) - Forest and Farm Facility

FAO is a specialised UN agency supporting governments and partners to design the right policies and programmes to end hunger, promote food security and promote sustainable agriculture.

FFF is a UN partnership providing direct financial support and technical assistance to strengthen Forest and Farm Producer Organizations (FFPOs). It empowers smallholders, women, youth, and Indigenous peoples to manage landscapes sustainably, improve livelihoods, and engage in climate change policy.

Grants

Family farmers and small-scale producers, including indigenous communities in rural territories.

Vulnerable populations facing food insecurity, malnutrition, and climate risks in Sierra and Amazon regions.

records.name: World Food Programme - Food Assistance for Assets (FFA)
records.summary:
The WFP is the world's largest humanitarian organisation, working to reduce hunger by providing emergency response, nutrition improvement and building community resilience.

The FFA initiative addresses the immediate food needs of vulnerable and food insecure people through cash, voucher or food transfers, also promoting the building of assets that will improve long-term food security and resilience.
records.intermediaries: Implementing partners include local NGOs as well as UN agencies such as FAO and IFAD.
records.implementers: Public. Funders include the USA, Japan, the EU, and others.
records.capital:
Cash-Based Transfers: Direct cash payments, often distributed via mobile banking or other electronic means, enabling beneficiaries to purchase food and essential items.
Vouchers: Exchangeable vouchers for food or specific goods.
records.instruments: National, subnational, jurisdictional, landscape · Climate adaptation, agriculture, food systems, agroecology
records.scale: Unclear
records.thematic: The FFA issues periodic calls for proposals via the UN Partner Portal.
records.size:
Indigenous peoples and rural populations at high risk of malnutrition, particularly in remote Sierra and Amazon regions.

Crisis-affected smallholder farming communities vulnerable to climate shocks, disasters, and food insecurity.

Family farmers and small-scale producers supplying national programs like Qali Warma school feeding
records.frequency:
Resilience enhancement through climate-adaptive food systems, including technical support for sustainable agriculture and disaster risk management.

Nutrition interventions for at-risk groups, such as fortified foods in school meals and anemia/stunting reduction pilots reaching thousands.

Public procurement from smallholders (mandated at 30% under new laws), linking family farming to school feeding and food banks for market access.
records.targetGroups:
Core Requirements
Activities focus on natural resource management, agricultural restoration, market access improvements, and skills training, emphasizing community participation, sustainability, gender equity, and alignment with national resilience plans.

Application Process
Proposals arise via WFP field assessments or partner collaborations, involving participatory planning and integration with government strategies rather than open public calls. · Entities (e.g. NGOs) must be registered on the UN Partner Portal to apply for funding. Funding proposals are  considered for any activity related to the design, implementation and management of asset creation activities (such as rehabilitating land or building water infrastructure) in exchange for cash or food transfers.
records.activities: The FFA relies on close coordination with national and local authorities. Its flexible design enables implementation in fragile or crisis-affected contexts where governance systems may be weak. FFA activities typically target natural resource management, agricultural restoration, market access improvements, and skills development, emphasizing community participation, sustainability, gender equity, and alignment with national resilience and recovery plans. The application process generally emerges from WFP field assessments or collaborations with partner organizations, using participatory planning to identify priorities and integrate with government strategies, rather than through open public calls.

records.name: Global Biodiversity Framework Fund (GBFF)
records.summary: The GBFF aims to help countries achieve the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework goals and targets with a strategic focus on strengthening national-level biodiversity management, planning, policy, governance, and finance approaches.
records.intermediaries: WWF, FAO,
records.implementers: Public
records.instruments: National · Biodiversity conservation, sustainable land use, NbS, agriculture linked to biodiversity protection
records.scale: Since 2024, the Global Environment Facility's Global Biodiversity Framework Fund (GBFF) has moved from launch to full-speed operation with over $288 million in projects approved
records.thematic: Operates on a structured cycle of selection rounds rather than fixed annual or periodic open calls. Deadlines are shown on website.
records.size:
Indigenous peoples and local communities managing forests and biodiversity-rich territories.
Community organizations and conservation groups involved in ecosystem stewardship.
Rural communities living near protected areas and biodiversity hotspots.
Local and national government institutions responsible for biodiversity conservation and protected-area management.
Community-based enterprises and initiatives linked to sustainable biodiversity use.
records.frequency:
Strengthening and expanding protected and conserved areas, including improved management of conservation landscapes and biodiversity corridors.
Ecosystem restoration and conservation of forests and biodiversity-rich landscapes.
Community-based conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, including stewardship of forests and ecosystems.
Development of bioeconomy and biodiversity-based livelihoods linked to sustainable resource use.
Support for national biodiversity strategies and implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
records.targetGroups:
Selection Criteria
1. Potential to generate Global Environmental Benefits
2. Alignment with the GBFF Programming directions and advancing the GBF implementation
3. Alignment with the NBSAP and BFP or similar instruments to identify national and/or regional priorities
4. Level of policy coherence and coordination across
multiple ministries, agencies, the private sector and civil society
5. Mobilization of private sector and philanthropies’ resources
6. Engagement with and support to IPLCs
7. Balance amongst regions · Accessible to national governments, international organizations, and accredited agencies of the Global Environment Facility (GEF).
records.activities: The GBFF’s enabling environment relies on countries having national biodiversity strategies and action plans (NBSAPs) aligned with the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF). Access to resources is determined by the degree of national policy alignment and institutional readiness to implement and monitor conservation priorities. Project selection further depends on the potential to generate measurable global environmental benefits; alignment with GBFF programming directions and the GBF’s goals; and consistency with national and regional priorities outlined in NBSAPs, Biodiversity Finance Plans (BFPs), or equivalent frameworks. The Fund also considers the level of policy coherence and coordination across government sectors, private sector engagement, and participation of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs), alongside efforts to mobilize co-financing from private and philanthropic sources and ensure a balanced regional distribution of investments.

records.name: Global Ecosystem-based Adaptation Fund
records.summary: The Global EbA Fund is a funding mechanism for catalytic, innovative, and inclusive projects that aim to create an enabling environment for the implementation of Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EbA) to enhance the resilience of vulnerable communities and ecosystems to the impacts of climate change.
records.intermediaries: National governments, NGOs, and local communities execute projects
records.implementers: Public
records.instruments: Landscape / subnational · Climate change adaptation, biodiversity conservation, sustainable agriculture, NbS
records.scale: The Global EbA Fund project portfolio is expected to grow up to a 100 grantees by the end of 2027. The portolio will include 90 small-sized grants with a funding envelope of up to USD 250,000 per project and 10 medium-sized grants with a funding envelope of up to USD 500,000 per project.
records.thematic: New calls for proposals and thematic tracks are announced in the Fund updates section.
records.size:
Smallholder farmers and rural producers adopting climate-resilient agricultural practices.
Indigenous peoples and forest-dependent communities managing landscapes and ecosystems.
Community-based enterprises and producer associations involved in sustainable value chains.
Local governments and territorial institutions responsible for adaptation planning and land-use management.
Women, youth, and vulnerable rural populations participating in sustainable livelihood initiatives.
records.frequency:
Ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA) measures such as restoration of forests, grasslands, and watersheds, sustainable land management, and conservation of ecosystems that support climate resilience.
Climate-resilient agriculture and natural resource management (e.g., sustainable livestock practices, agroecology, aquaculture, and management of non-timber forest products).
Development of sustainable rural livelihoods linked to ecosystem conservation, including nature-based enterprises and value chains.
Landscape-level investment planning and financing mechanisms to scale sustainable agriculture, conservation, and rural infrastructure.
Capacity building, governance strengthening, and support for adaptation planning and ecosystem management at territorial and community levels.
records.targetGroups:
Key Eligibility Criteria
Strictly qualifies as EbA per fund standards (nature-based solutions reducing vulnerability).
Duration ≤24 months (up to 36 with justification); innovative/upscaling potential; post-fund sustainability; specific climate risks addressed.
Lead complies with due diligence/financial capacity checks.

Application Process
Single-stage via online portal (globalebafund.smapply.io):
Eligibility Screening Questionnaire (checklist-based).
Due Diligence/Financial Capacity form + docs (e.g., registration, audits).
​
Full Application Form: logframe (1 outcome, ≤4 outputs/≤5 activities each), detailed budget, detailed activities table; all in English.
Consult Grants Procedures Manual first; calls have deadlines. · Legally recognized organizations (non-profits, NGOs, community groups, research institutions) as lead applicants, grounded in the project area with prior EbA experience; must partner with local institutions/communities and include gender/Indigenous perspectives. Projects must target vulnerable communities/ecosystems in developing countries; consortia encouraged but with one lead.
records.activities: The Fund targets initiatives that apply nature-based solutions to reduce climate vulnerability, emphasizing innovation, scalability, and long-term impact. While its effectiveness increases in countries with clear adaptation frameworks and institutional coordination, the Fund’s flexible design allows direct access for NGOs, facilitating implementation in diverse contexts. Eligibility centers on demonstrating genuine EbA approaches, credible financial and institutional capacity, and a clear plan for sustainability beyond the funding period. Its streamlined, competitive application process favors well-prepared proposals that can articulate measurable adaptation outcomes within a limited timeframe.

records.name: Climate Investment Funds (CIF)
records.summary: Through large-scale, low-cost, long-term financing, CIF lowers the risk and cost of climate investment, helping to get first-of-their-kind projects off the ground and contribute to transformational climate solutions.

records.implementers: Blended, including pledges from contributor countries and additional bilateral, private sector, MDB and other financing.
records.capital: Technical advisory and financial resources (including equity, grants, loans, guarantees, and local currency hedging)
records.instruments: National, subnational, landscape · Climate change mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity conservation, sustainable agriculture, NbS
records.scale: The DGM enables the extension of hundreds of micro-grants averaging USD 30,000.
records.thematic: Irregular, since the CIF follows a programmatic approach and solicits EOIs for programms on a need-basis.
records.size:
Indigenous peoples and forest-dependent communities in the Amazon.
Smallholder farmers and rural communities living in forest landscapes.
Community forest organizations and producer cooperatives.
Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in sustainable forestry or forest product value chains.
National and regional government institutions responsible for forest governance and land-use planning.
records.frequency:

Landscape restoration and sustainable land-use planning to protect forests and improve ecosystem management.
Support for sustainable forest-based livelihoods and value chains (e.g., non-timber forest products, sustainable forestry enterprises).
Strengthening forest information systems, climate monitoring, and institutional capacity for forest and land management.
Capacity building and policy support for climate-resilient land and forest management.
records.targetGroups: Countries must be selected as CIF partner countries and submit investment plans aligned with CIF programs (such as the Clean Technology Fund or Strategic Climate Fund). Applications are typically prepared in partnership with MDBs (e.g., World Bank, IDB, AfDB, ADB, EBRD), which help develop and submit projects for approval. Projects must demonstrate clear climate benefits (mitigation or adaptation), alignment with national climate strategies such as NDCs or NAPs, financial viability, and potential for scaling or transformational impact. · Accessible to national governments in developing countries through MDBs. Projects are developed jointly by governments and MDBs. Civil society organizations, private sector actors, and local communities cannot apply directly, but they may participate as implementing partners or beneficiaries within larger government-led programs
records.activities: CFI operate through multilateral development banks and depend heavily on robust national governance and policy frameworks. Countries must be designated as CIF partners and develop investment plans aligned with specific CIF programs—such as the Clean Technology Fund or the Strategic Climate Fund—typically in collaboration with MDBs. Access is driven by the strength of national climate strategies (e.g., NDCs, NAPs), sectoral alignment, and institutional readiness to implement large-scale investments. Projects are expected to deliver measurable mitigation or adaptation benefits, demonstrate financial soundness, and show clear potential for scalability and transformational impact.

records.name: PROFONANPE Environmental Fund
records.summary: PROFONANPE (Peruvian Trust Fund for National Parks and Protected Areas – Fondo de Promoción de las Áreas Naturales Protegidas del Perú) is Peru’s main environmental fund, a private, non‑profit institution that raises, manages, and channels financial resources for biodiversity conservation and climate‑change mitigation and adaptation. records.scale: Unclear

records.frequency:

Community resilience and sustainable livelihoods

records.name: AgroBanco
records.summary: Agrobanco is a state‑owned development bank of Peru created to provide financial services specifically to small‑ and medium‑scale agricultural and rural producers. It is the main instrument through which the Peruvian State channels credit and financial inclusion to the country’s agro‑sector, including agriculture, livestock, aquaculture, forestry, and agro‑industrial and export‑oriented activities.

records.frequency: Financing agricultural inputs and production cycles, supporting agricultural value chains and cooperatives, enabling investments in irrigation and technology, and promoting recovery and resilience of agricultural production in rural areas.

Typical application requirements include proof of land ownership or legal use of land, a basic production or investment plan, financial or credit information, and registration in relevant agricultural or tax systems. In many programs (such as the Fondo Agroperú), small farmers can apply individually or through organized groups like cooperatives or associations.

records.name: Agroideas
records.summary: Agroideas is a public‑sector program of the Ministry of Agrarian Development and Irrigation (Midagri) in Peru. Its main goal is to increase the competitiveness of small‑ and medium‑scale agricultural producers by supporting their organization, management, and adoption of technology through non‑repayable incentive funds.

records.activities: Depends on the public agricultural policy framework of Peru, as it is a government grant program. It requires institutional systems to allocate and manage funds but operates within an already established policy environment rather than depending on broader regulatory conditions.

records.name: Instituto Nacional de Innovación Agraria (INIA)
records.summary: INIA is the main public agricultural research and innovation institute of Peru, operating as a technical body under the Ministry of Agrarian Development and Irrigation (MIDAGRI). Its core mission is to strengthen Peru’s agricultural sector through scientific research, technology development, and the transfer of improved crop and livestock technologies to farmers.

records.activities: It is fully embedded in the national agricultural system and depends on government policies for research, innovation, and extension services. It operates as part of the enabling environment rather than relying on it externally.

records.name: Internation Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD)
records.summary: IFAD is a specialised UN agency and an international financial institution (IFI) dedicated to mobilising resources for agriculture and rural development in developing countries.
records.intermediaries: Typically national governments in partnership with local partners
records.implementers: Public. IFAD is funded by over 170 member states, as well as through philanthropy,
records.instruments: National and subnational · Climate mitigation and daptation, agroecology, biodiversity conservation, food systems and NbS
records.scale:
Small grants < USD 500,000
Large grants > USD 500,000

Smallholder farmers and family farming households in rural and highland regions.
Rural producer organizations, cooperatives and value-chain actors (e.g., coffee producers).
Indigenous peoples and rural communities in remote areas.
Rural entrepreneurs and small rural businesses.
Women and youth involved in agricultural livelihoods and rural enterprises.
Community organizations and local institutions involved in rural development.

Strengthening small-scale agriculture and livestock productivity through technical assistance, improved practices and diversified production systems.
Development of inclusive agricultural value chains (e.g., coffee and other rural products) and improving market access for small farmers.
Sustainable natural resource management and climate-resilient farming in rural landscapes.
Capacity building, training and technical services for rural producers and entrepreneurs.
Strengthening rural institutions, farmer organizations and territorial development initiatives.
Improving access to finance, markets and rural services through partnerships with the private sector and local service providers.
records.targetGroups: To access IFAD funding, countries must be IFAD member states and projects must align with national development priorities and IFAD’s objectives of reducing rural poverty, strengthening food systems, and supporting smallholder farmers and rural communities. Projects are usually designed jointly by governments and IFAD and may involve farmer organizations, NGOs, private sector actors, and research institutions as implementing partners. Application requirements generally include a government-led project proposal, feasibility and impact assessments, alignment with IFAD country strategies, and environmental and social safeguards, followed by appraisal and approval by IFAD’s Executive Board. · IFAD uses a performance-based allocation system (PBAS) to distribute funding to projects, which determine how much financing to allocate to a country based on its needs, performance and vulnerability.
records.activities: The enabling environment for IFAD operations is shaped by the strength and coherence of national rural development and agricultural policy frameworks, which determine the degree of strategic alignment and institutional readiness for implementation. Access to IFAD financing is limited to member states and depends on the consistency of proposed interventions with both national priorities and IFAD’s mandate to reduce rural poverty, strengthen food systems, and support smallholder farmers and rural communities. Given IFAD’s government-led delivery model, effective engagement relies heavily on domestic institutional capacity and cross-sector coordination, as projects are jointly designed by governments and IFAD in collaboration with farmer organizations, NGOs, private sector actors, and research institutions.

records.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
records.summary: The IDB Group has 26 borrowing member countries across Latin America and the Caribbean and provide financial and technical support to national and subnational governments and other entities in the region.
records.intermediaries: The IDB Group is also a partner and implementing agency itself with other development agencies and MDBs in several global thematic funds.
records.implementers: The IDB is owned by its 48 member countries and finances its operations by issuing bonds in international capital markets.
records.capital: Single-donor trust funds, thematic multi-donor funds, project-specific grants, parallel and joint co-financing of loans and grants, Balance Sheet Optimization instruments, Co-guarantee Agreements for credit enhancement of sovereign sustainable debt
records.instruments: National, subnational, landscape · Climate mitigation and daptation, agriculture, biodiversity conservation, food systems and NbS
records.scale: Recent investments include financing around USD 1 million to promote sustainable coffee farming practices among smallholder coffee farmers in Guatemala, and around USD 0.5 million in an  agroforestry project in Honduras.
records.thematic: The Bank regularly identifies projects to sponsor jointly with borrowing member countries, though no specific frequency is discernible.
records.size:
Smallholder farmers and rural agricultural producers adopting climate-smart practices.
Agricultural extension providers, research institutes, and innovation centers supporting farmers.
Water user associations and irrigation system managers.
Artisanal fishers and coastal communities dependent on marine ecosystems.
SMEs and private-sector actors in sustainable agriculture, bioeconomy, and green value chains.
National and local government institutions responsible for natural resource management and climate policy.
records.frequency:
Climate-resilient agriculture and agricultural innovation (technology transfer, research stations, climate-smart farming practices).
Irrigation modernization and water resources management in river basins and agricultural areas.
Coastal and marine ecosystem resilience, including climate adaptation for fisheries and coastal communities.
Biodiversity conservation, sustainable land management, and ecosystem protection (e.g., watershed management and conservation incentives).
Development of sustainable value chains and private-sector investment in agriculture and green businesses.
Institutional strengthening, policy reform, and capacity building for climate resilience and natural resource management.
records.targetGroups:
Core Requirements
Projects must target poverty reduction, inclusion, climate action, or innovation, with emphasis on vulnerable communities, sustainability, and partnerships; proposals require alignment with national priorities and often include co-financing or matching funds.

It is adviced to contact IDB country offices for program-specific calls; submissions typically involve concept notes, detailed budgets, and impact metrics reviewed for innovation, scalability, and feasibility. · Project finance is channeled through member borrowing countries.
records.activities: IDB's operations are most effective in countries with mature governance systems capable of managing complex, multisectoral investments. Its model hinges on strong public financial management, regulatory coherence, and institutional collaboration, as these conditions underpin the transparency and accountability required for large-scale financing. The IDB aligns its portfolio with national development and climate priorities, prioritizing interventions that combine poverty reduction, inclusion, and innovation with measurable climate and sustainability outcomes. Projects are assessed not only for technical soundness but also for their potential to catalyze systemic change through partnerships, co-financing, and policy integration.

records.name: IDB Invest
records.summary: IDB Invest is the private sector institution of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) Group, focused on financing sustainable enterprises and projects in Latin America and the Caribbean.

Public MDB capital leveraging private and institutional investors; blended/ concessional climate windows in some facilities.

It also depends on stable and predictable conditions that foster investor confidence and facilitate private sector participation.

records.name: Land Degradation Neutrality Fund
records.summary: The LDN Fund is an impact investment fund providing long-term financing (debt/equity) for sustainable land use projects that will reduce or reverse land degradation, mostly in the field of sustainable agriculture and forestry.
records.implementers: Public and private. Public donors include the European Investment Bank, the French Development Agency, DEFRA, the Government of Luxembourg, Global Affairs Canada (GAC) along with private investors Fondaction, Fondation de France, BNP Paribas Cardiff, Allianz, BPCE Vie, Garance and others. The fund is privately managed and run as an investment vehicle by primarily using public resources to cover investment risks and technical assistance.
records.capital: Long-term blended finance - primarily debt and equity
records.instruments: Landscape · Climate change mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity conservation, sustainable agriculture, NbS
records.scale: USD 300 million
records.thematic: Typically does not offer open calls for proposals; funding is targeted.
records.size:
Smallholder coffee producers organized into four cooperatives in Peru's degraded landscapes.
Producer cooperatives and small-scale farming groups seeking sustainable agriculture transitions.
records.frequency:
Reforestation and agroforestry of degraded land, integrating coffee with native trees for productive systems.

Sustainable land management to achieve land degradation neutrality, targeting 1.3 million metric tons of CO2 sequestration/reduction.

Value chain strengthening via technical assistance for cooperatives, including credit management and green coffee production models.
records.targetGroups:
Key Eligibility Criteria
Demonstrable LDN impact (monitor productivity, land cover, soil organic carbon).
Financial returns within 5-7 years, market-based (non-concessional), with detailed business model/value chain links.
Large-scale/replicable; flexible repayment/grace periods; agronomy/operations/governance strength.
​
Application Process
Multi-stage, invitation-based via Mirova (fund manager):
Submit Project Information Form (PIF), business plan, financial model, feasibility studies.
Preliminary review + NDA/data room; term sheet negotiation.
Due diligence (site visits, legal/financial checks); Expert/Investment Committee approval.
Contracting; optional Technical Assistance Facility (TAF/IDH-managed grants) for preparation. · Private-sector entities (businesses, project developers) with sustainable agriculture, forestry, or land restoration projects demonstrating economic viability, track record, and scalability.
Projects must target developing regions, contribute to SDG 15.3 (LDN), and meet high environmental/social standards; consortia possible but investees must be private
records.activities: The Fund functions at the intersection of environmental impact and commercial finance, making the enabling environment a decisive factor for investment viability. Secure land tenure, stable regulatory frameworks, and enforceable investment protections are prerequisites for structuring deals that can balance ecological restoration with private-sector risk-return expectations. The Fund targets projects capable of demonstrating measurable LDN outcomes, such as improved land productivity, soil carbon, and vegetation cover, through scalable, revenue-generating models. Given its non-concessional nature, financial viability within five to seven years is essential, placing a premium on strong agronomic performance, operational capacity, and governance integrity.

records.name: Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund
records.summary: The CEPF is a global biodiversity conservation fund that provides grants to civil society organizations working in the world’s most threatened biodiversity hotspots. Its role is to catalyze local conservation by supporting locally driven strategies, civil society leadership, and partnerships that protect ecosystems, species, and communities.
records.intermediaries: Local NGOs and civil society groups in biodiversity hotspots
records.implementers: Public and philanthropic. The fund is a joint program of l’Agence Française de Développement, Conservation International, the European Union, Fondation Hans Wilsdorf, the Global Environment Facility, the Government of Canada, the Government of Japan and the World Bank.
records.instruments: Regional and national · Biodiversity conservation, NbS

NGOs, universities, and research institutions working on biodiversity conservation.

Biodiversity conservation and ecosystem protection in Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) and conservation corridors in the Tropical Andes.

records.targetGroups:
To be considered for CEPF funding, a project must be located within a biodiversity hotspot where CEPF currently works. The list of eligible countries is listed under each open call for proposals. For project activities in a country that is not listed, checking with the CEPF Secretariat or the relevant regional implementation team before preparing an application is needed.
The project must also support at least one strategic direction outlined in the CEPF ecosystem profile for the hotspot. In addition, the project must not violate CEPF's safeguard policies.

Large grants are required to submit a letter of inquiry online, via a link in the call for proposals to the online grants management system. If the letter of inquiry is reviewed favorably, the fund will invite the organization to submit a full proposal. Proposals for large grants are typically, but not always, required to be written in English.
For small grants, an offline template (available in all of the languages specified in the call) will be provided. The application will be reviewed by CEPF's regional implementation team in the hotspot. Applicants for small grants are not required to prepare a full proposal. Any additional information required in support of the application (e.g., detailed budget, work plan, financial questionnaire, bank details) will be requested by CEPF's regional implementation team in the hotspot. · Accessible to civil society organizations, including NGOs, community-based organizations, Indigenous Peoples’ organizations, and academic institutions working on biodiversity conservation projects. Government-owned enterprises or institutions, are only eligible only if they can establish that the enterprise or institution:
- Has a legal personality independent of any government agency or actor
- Has the authority to apply for and receive private funds
- May not assert a claim of sovereign immunity
records.activities: The Fund functions within a generally supportive policy environment for conservation but stands out for its flexibility to fund civil society organizations directly, including in weaker governance contexts. Projects must be located within biodiversity hotspots where CEPF invests, align with at least one strategic direction in the ecosystem profile, and comply with safeguard policies.

records.name: Legacy Landscapes Fund (LLF)

Grantees are typically well-established NGOs with strong local roots, legal authorization to operate in the target landscapes, and a solid track record in large-scale conservation delivery. records.name: McKnight Foundation - Global Collaboration for Resilient Food Systems

McKnight, to support a wide range of grantmaking in the arts, environment, education, and basic human needs. Does the project demonstrate cultural and gender sensitivity?

Projects target tropical forest hotspots, prioritizing threat reduction (e.g., deforestation) and additionality—areas not already protected under IUCN I-VI categories. Indigenous-led groups are encouraged if they meet registration criteria.
